we recommend using Geo DNS

locations where you have distribution rights

claim: Latency data is based entirely on traffic between users and AWS data centers, so if you are not using resources in an AWS Region the actual latency between your users and your resources can vary significantly from AWS latency data.

evidence.quote: Data about the latency between users and your resources is based entirely on traffic between users and AWS data centers. If you aren't using resources in an AWS Region, the actual latency between your users and your resources can vary significantly from AWS latency data.

claim: If you do not create a default geolocation record, Amazon Route 53 returns a no answer response for queries from locations that it cannot identify or where you created no geolocation record.

values.display: Route 53 returns a "no answer" response

evidence.quote: If you don't create a default record, Route 53 returns a "no answer" response for queries from those locations.

note: d13-044. Pairs with the unmapped IP address sentence on the same page.

claim: For a domain or subdomain that is already in use, set a shorter TTL first (for example 300 seconds) and raise it after you confirm the new settings; a longer TTL means recursive resolvers use cached values longer before asking Amazon Route 53 for the latest information.
question: How does resolver caching delay a traffic shift between weighted records?

values.display: specify a shorter value first, such as 300 seconds

evidence.quote: However, if you specify a longer value for TTL, it takes longer for changes to the record (for example, a new IP address) to take effect. Recursive resolvers use the values in their cache for longer periods before they ask Route 53 for the latest information.

If you're changing settings for a domain or subdomain that's already in use, specify a shorter value first, such as 300 seconds, and increase the value after you confirm that the new settings are correct.

claim: If a record is associated with a health check, the guide says to specify a TTL of 60 seconds or less so that clients respond quickly to changes in health status.
question: What TTL should a health-checked record use?

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 weighted records with a health check

evidence.quote: If you're associating this record with a health check, specify a TTL of 60 seconds or less so clients respond quickly to changes in health status.

note: d13-045, d13-103, d13-104. The shared-values page words it 'we recommend that you specify a TTL of 60 seconds or less'.

claim: If a group of weighted records includes weighted alias records that route traffic to an ELB load balancer, specify a TTL of 60 seconds for the non-alias weighted records with the same name and type, because other values change the effect of the weights.
question: What TTL must non-alias weighted records use next to a weighted alias record for a load balancer?

values.display: specify a TTL of 60 seconds
the TTL for load balancers

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 weighted records that include an alias to an ELB load balancer

evidence.quote: If a group of weighted records includes one or more weighted alias records that route traffic to an ELB load balancer, specify a TTL of 60 seconds for all of the non-alias weighted records that have the same name and type. Values other than 60 seconds (the TTL for load balancers) will change the effect of the values that you specify for Weight.

claim: Before you change critical DNS entries, temporarily shorten the TTLs, make the change, observe and roll back quickly if needed, then raise the TTL again once the change works as expected.
question: How should you plan the TTL when you change a critical DNS record?

values.display: temporarily shorten the TTLs

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 record TTL best practice

evidence.quote: When you want to make changes to critical DNS entries, we recommend that you temporarily shorten the TTLs. Then you can make the changes, observe, and rollback quickly if you need to. After the changes are finalized and working as expected, you can increase the TTL.

note: d13-045, d13-103. Callvale: resolvers cache answers, so every change needs planning.

claim: For records that change as part of a rapid failover mechanism, especially health-checked records, lower TTLs are appropriate and a TTL of 60 or 120 seconds is a common choice; for delegation (NS) records and other rarely changed records longer TTLs are recommended.
question: Which TTL fits a health-checked failover record and which fits an NS record?

values.display: Setting a TTL of 60 or 120 seconds is a common choice
A value between an hour (3600s) and a day (86,400s) is a common choice

qualifiers.scope: Amazon Route 53 record TTL best practice

evidence.quote: For records that need to be altered as part of a rapid failover mechanism (especially records that are health checked), lower TTLs are appropriate. Setting a TTL of 60 or 120 seconds is a common choice for this scenario.

This is especially true on delegations (NS record sets), or other records that rarely change, for example MX records. For these records, longer TTLs are recommended. A value between an hour (3600s) and a day (86,400s) is a common choice.

claim: The typical TTL of an NS record is 172800 seconds (two days); if you do not lower it before migrating DNS to Amazon Route 53, your domain could be unavailable on the internet for up to two days if something goes wrong.
question: Why lower the NS record TTL before moving DNS service to Route 53?

values.display: 172800 seconds, or two days
unavailable on the internet for up to two days

qualifiers.scope: NS record TTL before a DNS migration

evidence.quote: The typical TTL setting for the NS record is 172800 seconds, or two days.
If you don't lower the TTL, your domain could be unavailable on the internet for up to two days if something goes wrong.

note: d13-103. Callvale: the NS record TTL at the registrar.

claim: When you migrate DNS to Amazon Route 53 the guide recommends lowering the NS record TTL to a value between 60 seconds and 900 seconds, then waiting two days after lowering it before switching name servers, and raising the TTL again afterwards.
question: Which NS TTL does the migration guide recommend and how long do you wait?

values.display: a value between 60 seconds and 900 seconds
wait for two days after you lowered the TTL

qualifiers.scope: NS record TTL during a DNS migration to Route 53

evidence.quote: We recommend that you specify a value between 60 seconds and 900 seconds (15 minutes).
To make sure that migrating DNS service to Route 53 happens all at one time, wait for two days after you lowered the TTL.
